props.title: Man on the Moon
props.initialSlug: Jim Carrey becomes Andy Kaufman in surreal biopic

sections.content: Jim Carrey's transformative portrayal of Andy Kaufman in **Man on the Moon** (1999) stands as one of cinema's most committed biographical performances. Director Milos Forman, who previously captured Mozart's genius in **Amadeus** (1984), brings similar psychological depth to Kaufman's avant-garde comedy. The film's meta-theatrical approach mirrors Kaufman's own blurring of reality and performance, predating similar fourth-wall breaking seen in **I'm Still Here** (2010) and **Exit Through the Gift Shop** (2010).

sections.content: The film's exploration of performance identity connects to other pivotal showbiz biopics like **Walk the Line** (2005) and **Ray** (2004), but Kaufman's story demands a more experimental approach. Forman and screenwriters Scott Alexander and Larry Karaszewski refuse to explain away Kaufman's eccentricities, instead embracing the enigma. This technique influenced later unconventional biopics like **I'm Not There** (2007), where multiple actors portrayed Bob Dylan's various personas. SUBHEAD: Comedy as Performance Art

Kaufman's wrestling persona and Tony Clifton character showcase how he transformed comedy into performance art, predating similar boundary-pushing seen in **Borat** (2006) and **Bruno** (2009). The film's behind-the-scenes footage, documented in **Jim & Andy: The Great Beyond** (2017), reveals how Carrey's method acting mirrored Kaufman's own commitment to staying in character, creating fascinating parallel narratives about performance and identity.
